messages.content:
You are evaluating a PTSD case vignette for the presence of causal
connections between five Ehlers & Clark cognitive components: Triggers, Negative Appraisals, Memory,
Threat, and Maladaptive Strategies.

For each of the 20 ordered, directed (A -> B) pairs of distinct components, decide whether the
vignette conveys, in some paragraph, that A influences, drives, or leads to B. Apply the same
causal standard as a structural validator:

COMPONENT SYNONYMS (any of these synonyms count as the component appearing):
  Triggers              -> "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals   -> "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory                -> "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat                -> "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies-> "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "safety behaviours", "maladaptive coping"

CAUSAL STANDARD
An edge A -> B is PRESENT (return 1) iff, within the same paragraph:
  (i) both A and B (or their synonyms) appear; AND
  (ii) the paragraph conveys that A influences / drives / leads to B, through direct causal
       language, sequential structure, or connecting phrases like "because of", "this meant",
       "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
If no paragraph conveys the A -> B relationship, return 0 for that edge.

You will return a binary judgement for each of the 20 ordered pairs. Be strict: do not assume
an edge based on mere co-occurrence; the paragraph must actually convey directional influence.

Evaluate the following vignette and judge each of the 20 directed edges
(A -> B) on whether the vignette conveys A influencing B.

VIGNETTE
Nadia Haddad is a 45-year-old auditor who came to treatment after years of trying to contain what began during a combat deployment and never really ended. She describes one attack in particular as the center of it, though even when she tells it she does so in fragments. Her convoy had stopped in an exposed stretch of road when there was a sudden explosion, a concussive bang that she still feels in her chest before she can think. She remembers turning toward the sound, dust and shouting, and catching the sharp scent of cologne from a man near her just before the scene broke apart in her mind. What torments her is not only what she recalls, but what she cannot. She knows there are missing sections she cannot force back. The memory comes as disconnected pieces-noise, scent, open sky, the feeling of being responsible for people around her-and the gaps have become as important to her as the pieces themselves.

In the years since, those pieces are easily stirred. She wakes from nightmares with the residue of the dream clinging to her, already scanning the room before she is fully awake. At work, if a client passes by wearing a particular cologne or perfume, she is abruptly back inside the emotional atmosphere of that day, with flashes of the event arriving without order. Unexpected bang sounds-construction outside the office, a slammed metal door in the parking garage-can bring the same effect. In those moments, the broken quality of the memory becomes more obvious to her, as if the trigger activates only shards and leaves the rest inaccessible, and that incompleteness quickly hardens into the old judgment that she failed to protect others. She has come to believe that if she were not the sort of person who freezes, misses things, or lets people down, she would remember clearly and would have acted differently. Once she is thinking this way, ordinary ambiguities stop feeling ordinary; a whiff of scent, a sudden noise, even someone moving quickly at the edge of her vision catches and holds because her own conclusions about herself and danger make them feel like signals she cannot afford to dismiss. Just as frightening to her is how fast her body reacts; she experiences that surge as proof that her body is now an enemy, still acting as though danger is present.

Those meanings have shaped how she lives. Because Nadia is certain there was some essential failure in her, she spends a great deal of time thinking about how life would have been different if the attack had not happened, replaying alternate versions in which she noticed more, moved faster, protected someone. That mental habit never resolves anything; it leaves her more convinced that the event revealed something bad about her character. She avoids open or exposed spaces with particular rigidity, choosing walls and corners in restaurants, declining outdoor gatherings, and taking indirect routes through her office so she does not have to cross the bright open lobby. As an auditor, she often visits client sites, and she plans those visits around where exits are, whether a conference room has a second door, and how quickly she could leave if she had to. She checks behind her in hallways, studies reflective surfaces for movement, and constantly scans for threat. The more she does this, the smaller her safe world becomes, until only a few places-her bedroom with the door locked, one interior office at work, her parked car before she steps out-feel even temporarily manageable. Living with that level of danger in her body has come to feel like proof in itself; if she is this afraid this often, she thinks, then perhaps she really is damaged, permanently changed, and not the kind of person who can trust herself anymore. The constant threat that shadows ordinary days has become one of the main things convincing her that something is fundamentally wrong with her, because she reads her own fear as evidence about her character rather than as a reaction she can understand.

That constriction has fed back into the trauma itself. Because Nadia spends so much energy monitoring surroundings and preparing escape routes, ordinary sensations are noticed and amplified; a faint perfume in an elevator, the echo of a dropped box in a stairwell, or the jolt of waking from a nightmare are immediately treated as signs that something is wrong. Once she is on alert, the threat feels current, not remembered. At that pitch, the convoy is suddenly close again; the sense that danger is present now seems to pull the attack back into her mind in fragments, as if staying keyed up keeps the memory active and ready to break through. Already running at that pitch, she finds the world thick with reminders she might once have ignored; the background sense of danger makes more and more cues feel personally relevant, as though nearly anything could turn out to be the next warning. In that state she reaches again for the same strategies-avoid the atrium, sit near the exit, scan every entrance, rehearse how to get out-and the act of living this way seems to confirm her fear that safety exists only in narrow zones. It also keeps her attention fixed on danger cues rather than on the fuller context of what happened, so the memory remains disjointed. The missing parts then become further evidence, in her mind, that she failed in some irreversible way. She tells herself that a decent person would have protected others, would remember, would not still be reacting like this.

Recently the strain has become harder to hide. After waking from a nightmare and arriving at a client office already tense, she caught the scent of a familiar cologne in a conference room just as a construction blast sounded outside. She froze, then insisted on moving the meeting to a smaller interior room with a clear exit, spending the rest of the time checking the door and losing track of the discussion. The embarrassment afterward was acute, but worse was the conviction that this was exactly who she is now: someone unsafe, someone whose own body cannot be trusted. Being divorced, she has managed much of this alone, and the isolation has deepened her certainty that there are only a few places in the world where she can be safe. She sought help when she realized she was beginning to structure both work and home around avoiding exposure and waiting for the next jolt. What frightens her most is that the fragments, the vigilance, and the self-blame will keep tightening until there is no life left outside those few safe zones; what she hopes, cautiously, is to stop feeling as though every bang, every scent, and every awakening is pulling her back into the same unfinished moment. Each time she has to rely on those routines to get through an ordinary task, it lands as further evidence that something in her is no longer intact; the very fact that she still needs the checking and escape planning strengthens her belief that she cannot cope the way other people do.

output.rationale: Causal connections are evident for most paths except Negative_Appraisals->Memory, Memory->Triggers, Memory->Maladaptive_Strategies, and Maladaptive_Strategies->Triggers.
